title: References and further reading
text: These references explain the statistical ideas behind the guides. A citation is not a claim that Trex implements every estimator, assumption, inference procedure or computational refinement in the cited work. The API reference and each guide’s scope section describe the implementation actually provided.

title: References and further reading
text:
Regression and moment restrictions

Hansen, L. P. (1982). Large Sample Properties of Generalized Method of Moments Estimators. Econometrica 50(4), 1029–1054. DOI.
Newey, W. K., and K. D. West (1987). A Simple, Positive Semi-Definite, Heteroskedasticity and Autocorrelation Consistent Covariance Matrix. Econometrica 55(3), 703–708. DOI.
Newey, W. K., and R. J. Smith (2004). Higher Order Properties of GMM and Generalized Empirical Likelihood Estimators. Econometrica 72(1), 219–255. DOI.
Muandet, K., W. Jitkrittum, and J. Kübler (2020). Kernel Conditional Moment Test via Maximum Moment Restriction. UAI. Proceedings.
Optimal Convex M-Estimation for Linear Regression via Antitonic Score Matching. The R package asm documents the original procedure and references. Trex ports its core score-learning idea; its numerical options and inferential implementation are not a claim of complete feature parity with the R package.

For least squares, Frisch–Waugh–Lovell projections, sandwich covariance and identification, a graduate econometrics treatment is useful alongside the worked code. GMM and kernel criteria require valid moments; automatic differentiation supplies derivatives, not identifying assumptions.

title: choice.base.ChoiceModel
text:
Guide & worked example · Source
Base class for structural discrete choice models.
This abstract class provides the foundation for implementing utility-based choice models such as logit, probit, and multinomial logit. All subclasses must implement methods for predicting choice probabilities, simulating choices, and performing counterfactual analysis.
Inherits from MaximumLikelihoodEstimator, which provides: - fit() method for parameter estimation via optimization - Standard error computation via Fisher information - Model summary statistics
Subclasses must implement: - _negative_log_likelihood(): Model-specific likelihood function - _compute_fisher_information(): Fisher information matrix computation - predict_proba(): Predict choice probabilities - simulate(): Simulate choices from the model - counterfactual(): Perform policy/counterfactual analysis

Fit the model using maximum likelihood estimation.
Optimizes the model parameters to minimize the negative log-likelihood using the specified PyTorch optimizer. After convergence, computes standard errors via the Fisher information matrix.
Args: X: Design matrix of shape (n_samples, n_features). Assumes X includes an intercept column if desired. y: Target vector of shape (n_samples,). init_params: Initial parameter values. For FE-aware GLMs, may be a packed parameter vector or a dict with coef and fe_coef. verbose: If True, prints convergence information. fe: Optional list of 1D fixed-effect ID vectors. fe_design: Optional list of sparse fixed-effect incidence matrices. hdfe_index: Optional index of the FE block to use for fast inference. offset: Optional offset vector added to the linear predictor. batch_size: Optional mini-batch size for first-order optimizers. stderr: Whether to compute standard errors.
Returns: Self (fitted estimator) with populated params dictionary.
Examples: >>> model = LogisticRegression() >>> model.fit(X_train, y_train, verbose=True) >>> print(model.params[“coef”])

title: choice.LowRankLogit
text:
Guide & worked example · Source
Low-Rank Logit model for matrix completion style choice problems.
This model handles varying choice sets (assortments) by learning a low-rank factorization Θ = AB^T of the user-item utility matrix, where users choose from presented assortments according to multinomial logit probabilities.
Based on: Kallus & Udell (2016), “Revealed Preference at Scale: Learning Personalized Preferences from Assortment Choices”

choice.LowRankLogit.counterfactual(
    user_indices,
    baseline_assortments,
    counterfactual_assortments,
    item_revenues=None,
)
Perform counterfactual analysis comparing two assortment scenarios.
This method evaluates the impact of changing the choice set (assortment) on market shares, choice probabilities, and optionally expected revenues. The low-rank structure allows heterogeneous user preferences, avoiding the IIA problem of standard multinomial logit.
Args: user_indices: User indices to evaluate (n_obs,) baseline_assortments: Binary mask (n_obs, n_items) for baseline scenario counterfactual_assortments: Binary mask (n_obs, n_items) for counterfactual item_revenues: Optional revenue per item (n_items,). If provided, computes expected revenues under each scenario.
Returns: dict containing: - baseline_probs: Choice probabilities under baseline (n_obs, n_items) - counterfactual_probs: Choice probabilities under counterfactual - baseline_market_share: Average choice probability per item (n_items,) - counterfactual_market_share: Average choice probability per item - market_share_change: Change in market share (n_items,) - baseline_expected_revenue: Expected revenue under baseline (if revenues provided) - counterfactual_expected_revenue: Expected revenue under counterfactual - revenue_change: Change in expected revenue - baseline_choices: Most likely choice per user under baseline (n_obs,) - counterfactual_choices: Most likely choice per user under counterfactual
Example: >>> # Evaluate impact of adding a new product (item 5) to assortments >>> baseline = torch.ones(n_obs, n_items) >>> baseline[:, 5] = 0 # Product 5 not available in baseline >>> counterfactual = torch.ones(n_obs, n_items) # All products available >>> results = model.counterfactual(users, baseline, counterfactual) >>> print(f”Adding product 5 changes market share by {results[‘market_share_change’][5]:.2%}“)

title: Synthetic control and synthetic difference-in-differences
text:
Arrange outcomes as an N\times T matrix: controls first, treated units last; pre-treatment columns first, post-treatment columns last. N0 and T0 mark the ends of the control and pre-period blocks. These estimators assume a common treatment start and a complete outcome matrix. They are not a staggered-adoption or arbitrary missing-panel interface.
Difference-in-differences subtracts an average control trend. Synthetic control instead forms a weighted combination of donors whose pre-treatment outcomes match the treated unit. Synthetic DID combines unit weights \omega and pre-period weights \lambda:

\hat\tau=\sum_{i,t}\widetilde\omega_i\widetilde\lambda_tY_{it},\qquad
\widetilde\omega=(-\omega,\mathbf1/N_1),\quad
\widetilde\lambda=(-\lambda,\mathbf1/T_1).

The SDID donor fit allows an intercept: matching the evolution of outcomes does not require matching their level exactly. Time weights compare the controls’ pre-period outcomes to their average post-period outcomes. Ridge regularization and simplex constraints limit unstable extrapolation.

title: Synthetic control and synthetic difference-in-differences
text:
Arrange outcomes as an N\times T matrix: controls first, treated units last; pre-treatment columns first, post-treatment columns last. N0 and T0 mark the ends of the control and pre-period blocks. These estimators assume a common treatment start and a complete outcome matrix. They are not a staggered-adoption or arbitrary missing-panel interface.
Difference-in-differences subtracts an average control trend. Synthetic control instead forms a weighted combination of donors whose pre-treatment outcomes match the treated unit. Synthetic DID combines unit weights \omega and pre-period weights \lambda:

\hat\tau=\sum_{i,t}\widetilde\omega_i\widetilde\lambda_tY_{it},\qquad
\widetilde\omega=(-\omega,\mathbf1/N_1),\quad
\widetilde\lambda=(-\lambda,\mathbf1/T_1).

The SDID donor fit allows an intercept: matching the evolution of outcomes does not require matching their level exactly. Time weights compare the controls’ pre-period outcomes to their average post-period outcomes. Ridge regularization and simplex constraints limit unstable extrapolation.

title: Synthetic control and synthetic difference-in-differences
text:
The simplex subproblem
Trex solves subproblems of the form

\min_{w\ge0,\,\mathbf1'w=1}\|Aw-b\|_2^2+n\zeta^2\|w\|_2^2.

With an intercept, it centers the columns and target before the weight fit. The solver is a Frank–Wolfe algorithm, with an optional sparsification and refinement pass. Its stopping rule uses improvement in the objective; it is not a reported KKT/duality-gap certificate. Check stability to maxiter and min_decrease when an optimum lies near a simplex boundary. This is distinct from CrabbyMetrics’ synthetic-control implementation.

title: Synthetic control and synthetic difference-in-differences
text:
Assumptions, sensitivity, and inference
Good pre-treatment fit is useful evidence about prediction, but does not prove absence of treatment-specific shocks, spillovers, anticipation or donor contamination. Donor selection, intervention timing and outcome definitions remain research decisions. The historical estimate above should not be read as a new causal reanalysis simply because it can be reproduced in Torch.
Examine donor concentration, pre-period residuals, placebo interventions and changes to the donor pool. Select tuning parameters without using treated post-treatment outcomes. Trex exposes point estimates and weights; it does not automatically provide the bootstrap, jackknife or placebo uncertainty procedures used in the SDID literature. Repeated-cell regression standard errors are not a substitute for a justified panel inference procedure.

title: Learning a robust regression score
text:
For a location regression Y=X'\beta+\varepsilon with density f, let \psi(e)=\partial_e\log f(e). The likelihood equation is \sum_i X_i\psi(Y_i-X_i'\beta)=0. A Gaussian density gives a linear score and least squares. Other error shapes suggest different weighting of large residuals, but estimating an unrestricted density derivative can be unstable.
Trex estimates a decreasing (antitonic) score. If \rho'(e)=-\psi(e), then a decreasing score makes \rho convex. This is a shape restriction on the score, not a claim that every heavy-tailed density has a decreasing score. In particular, the exact Student-t score is not globally decreasing.

title: Learning a robust regression score
text:
What the implementation does
AntitonicScoreMatchingRegression starts from a least-squares or LAD pilot. It smooths residuals with a kernel density estimate, constructs a score using the estimated density on a quantile grid, applies a pooled-adjacent-violators monotonicity projection, and interpolates the resulting score. It alternates score estimation with regression updates a chosen number of times.
The symmetry option imposes an odd score. It is useful for symmetric errors, but can be inappropriate for skewed disturbances. bandwidth, k, and kernel_grid_size control density smoothing and numerical resolution. This estimator uses NumPy/SciPy on the CPU despite sharing the Trex interface.

title: Optional local language-model generators
text:
Trex’s optional wrappers turn numeric training rows into text and parse generated text back into numeric rows. SafetensorsLLMInContextGenerator.fit stores examples; it does not update model weights. sample loads a local or Hugging Face model/tokenizer, constructs few-shot prompts, generates text, and collects parseable rows.

text:
Setup and example
The examples on this page are not executed by the documentation build. They require an explicitly selected model, substantial model files and additional dependencies; the ordinary site build does not download weights or start adapter training. The core package imports these wrappers without eagerly importing Transformers or bitsandbytes.
Install the optional libraries into the environment in which the chosen model runs:
python -m pip install transformers safetensors accelerate peft bitsandbytes
Availability of four-bit loading depends on the installed library versions and hardware. Use a supported CUDA environment for QLoRA; do not infer MPS or CPU compatibility from a generic device parameter.
import numpy as np
from trex import SafetensorsLLMInContextGenerator

# A local model/tokenizer directory selected and downloaded separately.
model_directory = "/path/to/your/model"
training_rows = np.array([[24, 1, 12.5], [40, 0, 21.0], [33, 1, 17.2]])

    model_path=model_directory, examples=3, rows_per_prompt=4,
    max_new_tokens=256, max_attempts=10, temperature=0.7, device="cuda",
).fit(training_rows, column_names=["age", "employed", "income"])

section: Text likelihood is not a tabular likelihood
text:
Text likelihood is not a tabular likelihood
Tokenization, column order, numeric formatting and prompting all change the task seen by the language model. A probability for a sequence of tokens is not automatically a density for a continuous row. Parsing and rejection further change the distribution of returned samples. Record the model revision, tokenizer, prompt settings, sampling parameters, adapter and rejection behavior when comparing experiments.
Enforce schema and support restrictions after generation, and distinguish invalid output from a valid but unusual observation. A successfully parsed row need not satisfy accounting identities or structural restrictions. Check duplication and proximity to training examples; generative modeling does not establish privacy or absence of memorization.

title: Optional local language-model generators
text:
When is this useful?
These wrappers make it possible to explore whether pretrained language-model representations help with a narrowly specified numeric simulation task. They are not the default recommendation for ordinary low-dimensional tabular data. Compare against empirical resampling, parametric baselines, mixtures, and tabular GAN/diffusion models, accounting for model loading and adaptation cost.
HTTP serving, prompt experiments and llama.cpp endpoint orchestration are outside this package API. These classes use the Transformers/safetensors route directly.

title: Binary and count likelihoods
text:
Binary and count outcomes require means in an appropriate range. Logistic regression uses p_i=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(x_i'\beta) and minimizes

L(\beta)=\sum_i\left[\log(1+e^{x_i'\beta})-y_ix_i'\beta\right].

Poisson regression uses \mu_i=\exp(x_i'\beta+o_i), where o_i is a known offset, and minimizes \sum_i[\mu_i-y_i(x_i'\beta+o_i)] up to outcome-only constants. An exposure e_i enters as o_i=\log e_i; it is not another coefficient to estimate.
The coefficient of a continuous variable is a log-odds slope in logit and a log-mean slope in Poisson. It is not the same as an additive probability or count effect. For logit, \partial p_i/\partial x_{ik}=p_i(1-p_i)\beta_k.

title: Binary and count likelihoods
text:
Additive effects and computational choices
These two GLM classes support fixed-effect ID blocks through fe, sparse incidence designs through fe_design, and offsets. The linear index becomes x_i'\beta+\sum_d\alpha^{(d)}_{g_d(i)}+o_i. Prediction must supply the matching FE inputs; unseen levels do not have an estimated effect. This is a likelihood fit with nuisance effects, not ordinary linear demeaning followed by a GLM.
The default optimizer is LBFGS. First-order optimizers can use batch_size for supported GLMs. stderr=False skips the information calculation when only fitting or prediction is desired. Sparse effects can reduce representation cost, but inference and nuisance blocks may still impose substantial memory costs.

title: Binary and count likelihoods
text:
Statistical qualifications
Model-based information is \sum_i p_i(1-p_i)x_ix_i' for ordinary logit and \sum_i\mu_i x_ix_i' for ordinary Poisson. These are not general heteroskedasticity/cluster-robust covariance estimators. A correct Poisson mean can motivate a quasi-likelihood point estimate under non-Poisson variance, but its reported model-based SE then needs separate justification.
Complete or quasi-complete separation can send binary-model coefficients toward infinity. Fixed effects with few observations per level introduce incidental-parameter concerns; no general bias correction is supplied. A large batch count or a small loss change does not resolve these statistical issues.
For probit, multinomial outcomes and factorized assortment choice, continue to static choice. API: LogisticRegression, PoissonRegression, MaximumLikelihoodEstimator.

title: K-nearest-neighbor grouped fixed effects
text:
Grouped fixed effects approximate a unit-specific latent process with a finite number of types:

Y_{it}=X_{it}'\beta+\alpha_{g(i),t}+\varepsilon_{it},\qquad
g(i)\in\{1,\ldots,G\}.

Compared with unit-by-time effects, grouping leaves variation with which to estimate slopes. Compared with additive unit effects, it allows type-specific time paths. The trade-off is approximation error and uncertainty about group membership. Increasing the number of groups can reduce approximation bias while leaving little within-group variation.
Trex constructs unit-level features, smooths them across nearest neighbors, clusters the smoothed features, and fits a linear model absorbing group-by-time indicators. The default feature construction stacks the panel history of covariates and, unless disabled, outcomes. Alternatively supply purpose-built unit-level classification features. This is a particular KNN-smoothed implementation, not every estimator covered by the grouped-FE literature.

text:
Worked example: an auxiliary type measurement
The simulation includes a noisy auxiliary measurement of each unit’s latent time path. This makes classification informative by construction; it is not evidence that arbitrary empirical clustering will recover meaningful types.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from trex import KNNGroupedFixedEffects

torch.set_num_threads(1)
torch.manual_seed(505)
N, T, G = 60, 8, 3
unit_ids = torch.arange(N).repeat_interleave(T)

                             use_flash_kmeans=False, seed=4, device="cpu")
fit.fit(X, y, unit_ids, time_ids, classification_features=features,
        classification_unit_ids=torch.arange(N))

text:
Design decisions and inference
The neighbor count controls smoothing, while the number of clusters controls the discreteness approximation. Standardizing embeddings changes what Euclidean closeness means. Large-scale searches are chunked; optional flash-kmeans acceleration is not required by the example and may have additional hardware/dependency requirements.
Using outcomes to form groups is not automatically invalid, but inference must account for estimated classification and the relevant asymptotic regime. The final absorbed-regression covariance is conditional on the estimated grouping; it is not a general post-clustering uncertainty guarantee. For an evaluation study, keep validation outcomes out of classification and compare against simpler additive FE and prespecified groups.
predict(X) returns the slope component, not arbitrary new-unit group effects. Group labels can permute across runs without changing the partition; compare co-membership or fitted paths rather than label integers.

A generator can match many marginal summaries while distorting overlap, tail behavior, conditional moments or the sampling distribution of an estimator.
Trex provides three differentiable tabular generators with optional context variables. Fit preprocessing only on the training sample and use the same transformation on validation, test and generated rows.

title: Tabular generators: WGAN, PTGAN, and diffusion
text:
Objectives and sampling

WGAN with a gradient penalty
A critic distinguishes real and generated rows through an approximation to the Wasserstein dual:

\max_D E[D(X)]-E[D(G(Z))]
-\lambda_{\rm GP}E[(\|\nabla_{\widetilde X}D(\widetilde X)\|_2-1)_+^2].

The generator minimizes -E[D(G(Z))]. TabularWGAN alternates critic and generator updates, with configurable network sizes, update ratio, Adam or optimistic Adam, and a one-sided gradient penalty (only norms above one are penalized). This differs from the two-sided penalty in the original WGAN-GP paper. The penalty is an approximate Lipschitz control, not a numerical certificate of exact Wasserstein distance.


Parallel-tempered GAN
TabularPTGAN trains across convexly tempered target laws Q_\alpha=\alpha X_1+(1-\alpha)X_2, conditioning its networks on the tempering coordinate. The endpoint \alpha=1 targets the original data distribution. The critic also receives a coherency penalty based on its directional derivative along paired data differences:

E\left[\{\nabla_qD(q,c_\alpha)'(X_1-X_2)\}^2\right].

This is distribution tempering in a GAN, not a replica-exchange MCMC algorithm. Context and noise interpolation have their own roles in training; sampling at a tempered interior coordinate produces a different target law. See the implementation and Sohn–Song paper before changing the penalty.


Denoising diffusion
TabularDiffusion adds Gaussian noise through a schedule:

X_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}X_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilon,
\qquad \min_\theta E\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(X_t,t,C)\|^2.

Generation starts from noise and iterates a learned denoising mean. Trex uses the schedule’s \beta_t as the sampling variance, with no final-step noise. This is a small DDPM-style model, not a likelihood-evaluating flow or an exact posterior sampler. Check that the chosen schedule makes the terminal forward law reasonably close to the noise initialization.

text:
Conditional draws and mixed columns
fit(X, context=C) learns a distribution conditional on the supplied context representation. sample(n, context=C_new) requires one context row per requested draw. It does not estimate the marginal law of future contexts; the caller must specify or sample those separately. Avoid extrapolating to unsupported contexts without validation.
TabularTransformer standardizes continuous columns, keeps binary columns on their 0/1 scale, and can round binaries and clip nonnegative columns after inverse transformation. These are post-processing operations, not a mixed discrete/continuous likelihood, and can alter moments or dependence. There is no automatic categorical encoding or missing-value imputation.

title: Dynamic choice: NFXP and CCP inversion
text:
A decision changes both current utility and the distribution of future states. Let P_a(s,s') be a controlled transition matrix, u_\theta(s,a) flow utility, and \delta<1 the discount factor. Under independent type-I extreme-value choice shocks, a normalized integrated value function satisfies

V_\theta(s)=\log\sum_a\exp\left[u_\theta(s,a)+
\delta\sum_{s'}P_a(s,s')V_\theta(s')\right].

The Euler constant is absorbed into a common value normalization; it does not affect choice probabilities. The softmax of the choice-specific values gives p_\theta(a\mid s). A discount factor below one makes this Bellman map a contraction. Trex uses dense transition tensors of shape (n_states, n_choices, n_states).

title: Dynamic choice: NFXP and CCP inversion
text:
Two estimation routes
RustNFP maximizes \sum_i\log p_\theta(a_i\mid s_i), solving the Bellman fixed point inside likelihood evaluations. Stable log probabilities matter: adding a probability floor before taking logs can flatten gradients for very unlikely observations.
HotzMillerCCP first estimates conditional choice probabilities \hat p. With P_{\hat p}=\sum_a\hat p_aP_a, policy evaluation gives

(I-\delta P_{\hat p})V_\theta
=\sum_a\hat p_a u_\theta(s,a)-\sum_a\hat p_a\log\hat p_a.

This avoids repeated Bellman iterations during the second-stage criterion. Estimated CCPs still introduce sampling error. Sparse state-action cells, smoothing, and first-stage approximation can strongly affect results. Trex’s post-fit predict_proba re-solves the structural model rather than returning the empirical first-stage probabilities.

section: Worked example: replace a deteriorating machine
text:
Worked example: replace a deteriorating machine
Keeping the machine costs \theta_m s; replacement costs \theta_r. Replacement mostly resets the state. We generate decisions from an independent NumPy Bellman calculation, hold the transition law fixed, and estimate both cost parameters. This is a small correctness illustration, not Rust’s original bus data or an empirical demand estimate.


Show Python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.special import logsumexp, softmax
from trex.choice import RustNFP, HotzMillerCCP, ReplacementUtility, DynamicChoiceData

torch.set_num_threads(1)
rng = np.random.default_rng(604)
S, discount = 8, 0.9
P = np.zeros((S, 2, S))
for s in range(S):
    P[s, 0, s] += 0.25
    P[s, 0, min(s+1, S-1)] += 0.75
    P[s, 1, 0], P[s, 1, 1] = 0.8, 0.2
truth = np.array([0.12, 2.0])
u = np.c_[-truth[0]*np.arange(S), np.full(S, -truth[1])]
value = np.zeros(S)
for _ in range(1000):
    new = logsumexp(u + discount*np.einsum("sat,t->sa", P, value), axis=1)
    if np.max(np.abs(new-value)) < 1e-12:
        value = new
        break
    value = new
prob = softmax(u + discount*np.einsum("sat,t->sa", P, value), axis=1)
rows = []
for individual in range(160):
    state = int(rng.integers(S))
    for time in range(45):
        action = int(rng.choice(2, p=prob[state]))
        next_state = int(rng.choice(S, p=P[state, action]))
        rows.append((state, action, next_state, individual, time))
        state = next_state
columns = torch.tensor(np.array(rows), dtype=torch.long).T
data = DynamicChoiceData(*columns)
models = {}
for name, cls in [("NFXP", RustNFP), ("CCP", HotzMillerCCP)]:
    model = cls(S, 2, discount, maxiter=120, tol=1e-8, device="cpu")
    model.set_transition_probabilities(torch.tensor(P))
    model.set_flow_utility(ReplacementUtility(device="cpu"))
    model.fit(data, init_params=torch.tensor([0.1, 1.8], dtype=torch.float64))
    models[name] = model
pd.DataFrame({"Truth": truth, **{name: m.params["coef"].detach().numpy()
                                 for name, m in models.items()}},
             index=["Maintenance cost", "Replacement cost"]).round(4)

title: Dynamic choice: NFXP and CCP inversion
text:
A policy counterfactual
Reducing replacement cost changes continuation values as well as current utility. counterfactual re-solves the model and can simulate new paths without mutating fitted baseline parameters. It starts each individual at their earliest observed state. Supply an explicit horizon for an unbalanced panel.


Show Python
model = models["NFXP"]
states = torch.arange(S)
baseline = model.predict_proba(states).detach().numpy()
old_coef = model.params["coef"].clone()
cf = model.counterfactual(
    data, {"theta_replacement_cost": float(old_coef[1])*0.5},
    rng=torch.Generator().manual_seed(70), n_periods=20,
)
changed = cf["counterfactual_probs"].detach().numpy()
assert torch.equal(old_coef, model.params["coef"])
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(np.arange(S), prob[:, 1], "k:", label="DGP probability")
ax.plot(np.arange(S), baseline[:, 1], "o-", label="Fitted baseline")
ax.plot(np.arange(S), changed[:, 1], "o-", label="Lower replacement cost")
ax.set(xlabel="Deterioration state", ylabel="Replacement probability", ylim=(0, 1))
ax.legend(); plt.show()

What this does not establish
The example conditions on known transitions and a fixed discount factor. If transitions are estimated, their uncertainty belongs in inference. title: Econometric models in PyTorch
text:
Trex brings familiar econometric objectives into tensor-based workflows: least squares with fixed effects, moment restrictions, choice probabilities, panel counterfactuals and learned simulation models.
The library is useful when an estimator needs to share data, derivatives or hardware with a PyTorch model. It is also a research collection: interfaces, computational costs and available inference differ across modules. These guides explain those distinctions alongside worked examples.

title: Econometric models in PyTorch
text:
A recommended reading path

Install from the repository. The unrelated PyPI package named trex is not this library.
Work through the quickstart and numerical conventions.
Pick a method by its assumptions and target, not merely its ability to fit a tensor. Every method guide connects a criterion to code, diagnostics and interpretation.

title: Econometric models in PyTorch
text:
What the examples establish
Numerical vignettes execute against the documented source and show their actual results. Small synthetic examples illustrate identification and computation; they are not broad claims about estimator rankings or accelerator speed. The panel vignette additionally uses the attributed California Proposition 99 fixture.
The reference-test record documents comparisons with R, Statsmodels, SciPy and linearmodels. Dynamic-choice and low-rank-logit standard errors are not implemented; generative-model fit quality does not establish causal validity. These limits are discussed where they affect an example.
Build provenance records the source revision and software environment used for this site. Contributing explains how documentation changes reach gh-pages.

title: Choosing an estimator
text: Choose the restriction you can defend and the output you need. A flexible fit is not by itself an identification argument.

title: Choosing an estimator
section: Estimation, prediction and inference are different capabilities
text:
Estimation, prediction and inference are different capabilities
Dynamic choice and low-rank logit have prediction interfaces but no implemented standard errors. Neural conditional moments and factorized panel models do not provide a generic valid confidence interval merely because gradients exist. SC/SDID here return point estimates, not automatically valid placebo or bootstrap intervals. The linear estimator does not implement clustered covariance.
If the goal is a causal panel effect, distinguish an observation mask from an untreated-training mask. Matrix completion and latent-factor GLMs fit whichever cells they receive. A good held-out-cell score does not prove accurate extrapolation to a treated block.

title: Choosing an estimator
text:
What belongs elsewhere
Trex is not a formula parser, missing-data imputation policy, experiment randomization engine, or a complete causal-identification framework. It does not offer every estimator found in its research notebooks as a stable public class. The separate Gaussian-tabular pilot and policy-aligned CATE proposal are not documented as merged API features.
For all public entry points—including preprocessing, transition estimation and result structures—see the API index.

title: Devices, precision and inference
text:
Most cross-sectional estimators take a design X of shape (n, p) and outcome y of shape (n,). Multinomial logit uses one-hot y of shape (n, J). Dense panel models use outcomes (units, times) and, when needed, covariates (units, times, p). Dynamic choice has integer states/actions and a transition tensor (states, actions, next_states).
Add intercepts explicitly except where the documented estimator supplies its own (AntitonicScoreMatchingRegression defaults to one). Reject or handle missing observations before ordinary regression. For panel masks, True means included in fitting.

title: Devices, precision and inference
text:
Precision and devices
Base estimators choose CUDA when available, otherwise CPU. Pass device="cpu" or device="cuda" explicitly for reproducibility. Float64 is a sensible starting point for ill-conditioned moments, Bellman derivatives and covariance calculations; fixed-effect absorption and GMM use double precision internally. Apple MPS does not support float64 and is not a drop-in backend for those methods.
GEL and antitonic score estimation perform substantial work in NumPy/SciPy. A tensor input does not guarantee GPU-resident computation. Device transfers, small matrix sizes, kernel launch overhead and dense kernel/transition storage can dominate runtime. Measure an actual workload before assuming acceleration.

title: Devices, precision and inference
text:
Objectives and covariance scaling
Optimization gradients and inferential covariance solve different problems. If \bar g_n(\theta)=n^{-1}\sum_i g_i(\theta), the inverse curvature of a mean criterion is not automatically the finite-sample covariance. GMM reports

\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\theta)=\frac1n
(G'WG)^{-1}G'W\widehat\Omega WG(G'WG)^{-1}.

Its covariance_ includes 1/n; legacy vtheta_ does not. Likelihood models use their implemented Fisher-information calculation, not a generic robust sandwich. A Poisson conditional mean can be useful under overdispersion while its model-based standard errors are inappropriate. HC1 in linear regression is heteroskedasticity-robust, not serially or cluster robust.

title: Devices, precision and inference
text:
Optimization diagnostics

Inspect objective histories and sensitivity to starting values for nonconvex models.
Compare more iterations and reasonable tolerances; small objective changes need not imply a unique or identified estimate.
Check rank, overlap and support before optimization. Numerical regularization changes an objective; it does not establish identification.
Distinguish probabilities from log probabilities. Stable log_softmax and log-CDF calculations matter especially for rare choices.
Seed every experiment and record versions. CPU/CUDA results can differ without either being wrong; test appropriate numerical tolerances rather than bitwise equality.

These examples are deliberately small, generally single-seed demonstrations. A substantive comparison needs repeated DGPs/seeds, held-out evaluation, matched computational budgets and an explicitly chosen estimand.

title: Conditional moments: kernels and sieves
text:
Consider Y=h_0(T)+U, with E[U\mid Z]=0 but potentially E[U\mid T]\ne0. Ordinary prediction learns E[Y\mid T], not necessarily h_0. An instrument restriction instead asks whether the fitted residual is orthogonal to every function of Z. Identification still requires enough variation in the instruments: a flexible optimizer cannot supply completeness or instrument validity.
Trex connects a differentiable torch.nn.Module for h_\theta to a moment callback \rho_\theta=\rho(h_\theta(T),Y). For an IV regression, use \rho_\theta=h_\theta(T)-Y. Both estimators below operate on the complete sample; they are not stochastic-minibatch IV estimators.

title: Conditional moments: kernels and sieves
text:
Two finite-sample objectives
Maximum moment restriction (MMR) uses a positive-definite kernel:

Q_K(\theta)=\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i,j}
\rho_{\theta,i}'\rho_{\theta,j} k(Z_i,Z_j).

Trex uses an RBF kernel, with a median-distance bandwidth when none is given. This is the nonnegative, diagonal-including quadratic criterion, not an unbiased off-diagonal U-statistic. The kernel matrix costs O(n^2) memory. For vector-valued moments the objective sums the componentwise quadratic forms. Instrument scaling and bandwidth affect the criterion’s geometry.
Sieve minimum distance (SMD) replaces all instrument functions by a finite polynomial basis B_i=b(Z_i):

M_\theta=n^{-1}\sum_i B_i\rho_{\theta,i}',\qquad
Q_B(\theta)=\operatorname{tr}\left[
M_\theta'(n^{-1}B'B+rI)^+M_\theta\right].

Trex standardizes instruments before constructing the polynomial sieve. degree, interactions, and the ridge r determine the approximation. Increasing the degree can add weak or nearly redundant moments; it is not a free improvement in identification.

title: Conditional moments: kernels and sieves
section: Worked example: an endogenous nonlinear regressor
text:
Worked example: an endogenous nonlinear regressor
Here T=0.9Z+V and U=0.7V+\varepsilon. We know the response is quadratic and estimate its coefficients. This deliberately separates the instrument problem from neural-network approximation and local minima.


Show Python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from trex import MaximumMomentRestriction, SieveMinimumDistance

torch.set_num_threads(1)
torch.manual_seed(721)
n = 700
z = torch.randn(n, 1, dtype=torch.float64)

title: Conditional moments: kernels and sieves
text:
Diagnostics and scope
Inspect the fitted criterion and loss history, and evaluate moments on new observations. A small training loss can mean overfitting the instrument sample. Compare sensitivity to bandwidth or sieve degree on validation moments rather than selecting by in-sample loss alone. The hsic helper is a dependence diagnostic, not a replacement for an identification argument.
These classes do not supply a complete inferential procedure for learned functions. Their interfaces accept neural modules, but neither automatic standard errors nor causal validity follows from that flexibility. Account for regularization, approximation, weak instruments, and tuning in any inferential extension. For finite-dimensional unconditional moments and sandwich covariances, see GMM.
API: MaximumMomentRestriction, SieveMinimumDistance, mmr_loss, polynomial_sieve.

title: Generalized empirical likelihood
text:
GMM assigns a quadratic cost to violations of average moments. Generalized empirical likelihood instead introduces a multiplier vector that tilts the empirical distribution. For moments g_i(\theta) and a concave generating function \rho, the profiled criterion can be written

\hat\theta=\arg\min_\theta\sup_\lambda
\frac1n\sum_i\rho\bigl(\lambda'g_i(\theta)\bigr).

Trex implements empirical likelihood \rho(v)=\log(1-v), exponential tilting \rho(v)=1-e^v, and a quadratic/CUE-style form \rho(v)=-v-v^2/2. Additive constants do not affect the minimizer. The inner optimization, its domain and the outer parameter fit are distinct numerical problems.
Under valid, well-identified moments, these methods share first-order efficient GMM behavior. Their finite-sample and misspecification properties can differ. Changing the tilt is not a remedy for a false identifying restriction.

title: Generalized empirical likelihood
text:
Domain and covariance
For empirical likelihood, each \lambda'g_i must stay below one. Clipping arguments into this domain would change the optimization problem; Trex instead uses a feasibility-preserving line search. Exponential tilting can be numerically difficult for extreme moments. Failure to find a finite feasible optimum is reported rather than replaced by a fabricated estimate.
Let G be the Jacobian of average moments and \Omega=E[g_i g_i']. The implemented correctly specified first-order covariance is

\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\theta)
=\frac1n(G'\widehat\Omega^{-1}G)^{-1}.

It has parameter dimension p\times p, not moment dimension q\times q. Trex stores it as Sigma, with se its marginal standard errors. est holds coefficients and lam_hat the final multiplier vector. This calculation is not misspecification-robust GEL inference, nor necessarily the same finite-sample reweighted covariance returned by another package.
In just-identified problems, a root of the sample moments often makes the methods coincide; overidentification creates scope for their empirical weighting to matter. In applied work, compare moment definitions and normalization before attributing a discrepancy to an optimizer.
API: GELEstimator, EL, ET, CUE-style tilt. Background: Newey and Smith (2004); see references.

title: Instrumental variables and GMM
text:
Suppose a structural residual u_i(\theta) satisfies E[z_i u_i(\theta_0)]=0 even though a regressor is correlated with the residual. Define the observation-level vector g_i(\theta)=z_i u_i(\theta) and minimize

Q_n(\theta)=\bar g_n(\theta)'W\bar g_n(\theta),\qquad
\bar g_n(\theta)=\frac1n\sum_i g_i(\theta).

The weighting matrix decides how competing sample restrictions are reconciled. Identity weighting is simple; efficient two-step GMM estimates a moment covariance at a preliminary fit and then uses its inverse. Neither weighting choice can repair invalid instruments or weak identification.
Trex takes a callback moment_cond(z, y, x, theta) returning one row per observation, shape (n, q). Do not return only the average: observation-level moments are needed for covariance estimation.

title: Instrumental variables and GMM
text:
Weighting, dependence and inference
With G=\partial\bar g_n(\theta)/\partial\theta' and a consistent long-run covariance \widehat\Omega, the reported covariance is

\widehat V=\frac1n(G'WG)^{-1}G'W\widehat\Omega WG(G'WG)^{-1}.

Under independent sampling, Trex uses the uncentered second product n^{-1}\sum_i g_i g_i' (HC0 convention). With ordered, weakly dependent observations, iid=False uses Bartlett/Newey–West accumulation for both optimal weights and final inference:

\widehat\Omega=\widehat\Gamma_0+
\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\left(1-\frac{\ell}{L+1}\right)
(\widehat\Gamma_\ell+\widehat\Gamma_\ell'),\quad
\widehat\Gamma_\ell=\frac1n\sum_{i=\ell+1}^n g_i g_{i-\ell}'.

Set max_lags explicitly when a particular bandwidth is part of the design. Reordering the rows changes this calculation. HAC is not a substitute for an arbitrary cluster structure.

       "parameter_covariance_shape": list(m.covariance_.shape),
       "backend_coefficient_max_gap": float(np.max(np.abs(m.theta_-fits["scipy"].theta_)))})

title: Latent-factor generalized linear models
text:
An additive unit effect shifts every period equally. Interactive effects allow units to respond differently to common shocks:

\eta_{it}=X_{it}'\beta+A_i'B_t+o_{it},\qquad
E[Y_{it}\mid X,A,B]=g^{-1}(\eta_{it}).

LatentFactorGLM supports Gaussian/identity, Bernoulli/logit and Poisson/log families. The offset o_{it} is known, not estimated. Unit and time IDs index factor rows. The model does not automatically add separate unit and time intercepts: represent desired additive terms explicitly or choose an appropriate model specification.
Trex minimizes the mean observed-cell negative log likelihood, plus

\frac{\lambda}{2}\{\operatorname{mean}(A^2)+\operatorname{mean}(B^2)\}
+\frac{\lambda_\beta}{2}\operatorname{mean}(\beta^2).

The Gaussian loss is half the squared error. The factorization makes optimization nonconvex; factor rescalings and rotations also make individual factor coordinates non-unique. Interpret the product AB' or predicted means, not an arbitrary fitted axis as an identified economic trait.

Layout and limitations
Dense input uses X.shape == (N,T,p) and y.shape == (N,T). An observation list uses (n_obs,p) and explicit unit_ids and time_ids. A boolean mask selects training observations in either layout; predictions still require levels represented in the fitted model. This is not a cold-start embedding model for new units or dates.
Use multiple starts and time- or block-aware validation for rank and penalty. The current implementation does not report identification-aware coefficient or treatment-effect covariance estimates. With short panels, nonlinear incidental parameters can matter. Interactive effects are a model for unobserved heterogeneity, not by themselves a causal identification strategy.

title: Weighted regression and fixed effects
text:
Panel regressions often have a small number of slopes and many nuisance intercepts. In

y_{it}=x_{it}'\beta+\alpha_i+\gamma_t+\epsilon_{it},

the slope is identified by variation left after projecting out unit and time effects. Explicitly constructing thousands of indicator columns is usually unnecessary. Trex uses weighted alternating projections to residualize all design columns and the outcome together, then solves a least-squares problem.
For strictly positive analytic weights W=\operatorname{diag}(w_i), write \widetilde X and \widetilde y for weighted within-transformations. The estimate solves

\hat\beta=\arg\min_\beta\|W^{1/2}(\widetilde y-\widetilde X\beta)\|_2^2.

Alternating demeaning converges to the joint weighted projection; one subtraction of unit means and time means need not suffice in an unbalanced or unequally weighted panel. A failure to converge raises an error.

text:
What the uncertainty calculation uses
Set A=W^{1/2}\widetilde X and r=\widetilde y-\widetilde X\hat\beta. The supported covariances are

\widehat V_{\rm classical}=(A'A)^{-1}\frac{r'Wr}{n-k},
\qquad
\widehat V_{\rm HC0}=(A'A)^{-1}
\left(\sum_i w_i^2\widetilde x_i\widetilde x_i'r_i^2\right)(A'A)^{-1},

with \widehat V_{\rm HC1}=n\widehat V_{\rm HC0}/(n-k). Here k counts retained slope columns and the rank of absorbed effects. In a connected two-way panel, absorbed rank is N+T-1; disconnected support changes that count. For large three-or-more-way designs, supply df_absorbed when the exact-rank calculation exceeds the implementation’s level-space bound.

Interpretation and boundaries

predict(X) returns only X\hat\beta. fitted_values_ includes the estimated effects on the training rows. There is no new-level FE prediction interface in this class.
An intercept absorbed by FE retains a zero coefficient slot; zero does not mean the population intercept was estimated as zero.

Current choices are None, classical, HC0, and HC1. Repeated panel rows often need clustered inference, which is not implemented here.
A regressor with no within variation cannot identify a slope. Trex drops absorbed columns and rejects remaining rank deficiency.

title: Nuclear-norm matrix completion
text:
Write Y_{it}=a_i+b_t+L_{it}+\varepsilon_{it}, where L is approximately low rank. Shared latent factors allow observed cells to inform missing cells. Instead of choosing a rank and fitting factors directly, nuclear-norm regularization shrinks singular values:

\min_{a,b,L}\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\sum_{(i,t)\in\Omega}
(Y_{it}-a_i-b_t-L_{it})^2+\lambda_L\|L\|_*.

Here \Omega is the training set and \|L\|_* is the sum of singular values. Trex alternates additive-effect updates with singular-value thresholding. An explicit lambda_L controls the penalty; otherwise lambda_fraction scales a data-dependent maximum-penalty reference.
The mask uses True for observed/training cells. False cells do not contribute to the objective. A zero outcome is a value, not a missing-data marker. Low-rank imputation still requires informative observation patterns; entirely unsupported rows, columns or disconnected blocks are not rescued by calling a solver.

title: Nuclear-norm matrix completion
section: From prediction to a treatment effect
text:
From prediction to a treatment effect
The helper matrix_completion_estimate(Y, N0, T0) excludes the entire treated post-treatment block, fits untreated outcomes, and averages Y_{it}-\widehat Y_{it}(0) over that block. It returns the effect and fitted model. This prevents direct use of treated outcomes in training, but does not establish that their untreated counterfactual is identified.
Randomly holding out cells, as above, tests interpolation under a different missingness pattern from withholding a final treated block. For causal work, use block-aware validation and justify why those validation tasks transport to the intervention. An outcome-dependent observation process can also invalidate standard matrix-completion reasoning.

title: Nuclear-norm matrix completion
text:
Practical choices

Tune the penalty using a separate validation mask, then report final test error once. The fixed penalty above is an illustration, not a tuned result.
Inspect singular values, convergence history and residual structure. A tiny training error with poor held-out error signals excessive flexibility.
Choose whether unit and time effects belong in the model. They are unpenalized nuisance components here, distinct from the low-rank term.
The current estimator does not supply treatment-effect standard errors. Serial dependence and estimated factors need an explicit inferential plan.

For covariates and non-Gaussian outcomes with an explicit rank constraint, see latent-factor GLMs.
API: NuclearNormMatrixCompletion, MatrixCompletionResult, matrix_completion_estimate.

title: Static discrete choice
text:
A binary model observes Y_i=1\{X_i'\beta+\varepsilon_i>0\}. Logistic errors give P_i=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(X_i'\beta); standard normal errors give P_i=\Phi(X_i'\beta). Their coefficient scales differ because the latent error variances are normalized differently. Compare probabilities or marginal effects, not raw logit and probit coefficients.
Trex exposes BinaryLogit and BinaryProbit in trex.choice. The regression-family LogisticRegression additionally supports the fixed-effect and offset machinery described in GLMs.
For J alternatives, the multinomial model is

P(Y_i=j\mid X_i)=\frac{\exp(X_i'\beta_j)}
{\sum_{k=1}^{J}\exp(X_i'\beta_k)},\qquad \beta_J=0.

The last alternative is Trex’s reference category. X has shape (n,p), with the same observation-level covariates entering alternative-specific coefficient vectors. This is not a long-format conditional-logit formula API for arbitrary alternative-specific covariates.

Worked example: three alternatives

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from trex.choice import MultinomialLogit

torch.set_num_threads(1)
rng = np.random.default_rng(351)
n = 1200
x = rng.normal(size=n)
X = np.c_[np.ones(n), x]
beta = np.array([[0.3, -0.2], [1.0, -0.8]])
logits = np.c_[X @ beta, np.zeros(n)]
prob = np.exp(logits-logits.max(axis=1, keepdims=True))
prob /= prob.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
choices = np.array([rng.choice(3, p=p) for p in prob])
y = np.eye(3)[choices]  # MultinomialLogit expects one-hot outcomes.
fit = MultinomialLogit(maxiter=150, tol=1e-9, device="cpu").fit(
    torch.tensor(X), torch.tensor(y)
)
pd.DataFrame(fit.params["coef"].detach().numpy(),

The covariance corresponds to the free, non-reference coefficients. For a covariate x_k, the probability derivative is \partial P_j/\partial x_k=P_j(\beta_{kj}-\sum_\ell P_\ell\beta_{k\ell}). A positive utility coefficient need not mean every comparison of average probabilities increases: the entire choice set and covariate distribution matter.

title: Static discrete choice
text:
Low-rank preferences over assortments
When users and products repeat, LowRankLogit replaces an unrestricted utility matrix by \Theta=AB', with low-dimensional user and item factors. For a displayed assortment S_i,

P(j\mid u_i,S_i)=\frac{\exp(\Theta_{u_i j})}
{\sum_{k\in S_i}\exp(\Theta_{u_i k})},\quad j\in S_i.

An assortment is part of the conditioning information: an unavailable item is not an observed rejection. The factors are not separately identified under rotations. The rank and penalty regularize predictions, not automatically economic preference parameters. Below is a small full-assortment fit.


Show Python
from trex.choice import LowRankLogit

torch.manual_seed(13)
n_users, n_items, n_obs = 20, 6, 300
users = torch.randint(n_users, (n_obs,))
utility = torch.randn(n_users, 2) @ torch.randn(2, n_items) * 0.4
items = torch.multinomial(torch.softmax(utility[users], dim=1), 1).squeeze(1)
low_rank = LowRankLogit(rank=2, n_users=n_users, n_items=n_items,
                       lam=0.02, maxiter=80, device="cpu")
low_rank.fit(users, items)
print("Full-assortment probabilities for user 0:")
print(low_rank.predict_proba(torch.tensor([0])).detach().numpy().round(3))


Warning: Could not compute standard errors: LowRankLogit standard errors are not implemented; factor rotations make the naive Hessian singular
Full-assortment probabilities for user 0:
[[0.081 0.218 0.275 0.037 0.056 0.333]]

title: Static discrete choice
text:
Interpretation and checks
Report held-out log loss as well as classification accuracy. Check rare alternatives and separation; finite optimization does not establish a finite MLE. Multinomial logit imposes IIA conditional on included covariates; low-rank heterogeneity changes the model but does not eliminate all substitution restrictions. Neither fitting choices nor changing covariates identifies price elasticities without an exogeneity or identification argument.
Low-rank standard errors are not implemented. The static counterfactual helpers compare fitted probabilities; they do not solve a supply equilibrium.
API: BinaryLogit, BinaryProbit, MultinomialLogit, LowRankLogit.

Estimate state transition probabilities P(x’|x,a) from panel data.
Three approaches supported: 1. “frequency”: Nonparametric frequency estimator (implemented) 2. “kernel”: Kernel smoothing for continuous states (future) 3. “parametric”: Ordered probit/logit for ordinal transitions (future)

Example: >>> # Estimate transitions from bus maintenance data >>> P_hat = estimate_transition_matrix( … states=data.states, … actions=data.actions, … next_states=data.next_states, … n_states=90, … n_choices=2, … method=“frequency” … ) >>> # Verify probabilities sum to 1 >>> assert torch.allclose(P_hat.sum(dim=2), torch.ones(90, 2))

title: Development and documentation
text:
Build the site
Install Quarto 1.8.27 and the Python documentation extra. Use the same Python environment for the package, Quartodoc and executable examples:
python -m pip install -e '.[docs]'
python docs/build.py
The builder generates API pages with Quartodoc, checks coverage of public exports, records the source revision and environment, executes the vignettes, renders the website, and checks internal links and assets. Output goes to docs/_site/; it is not committed to the source branch. During writing:
python docs/build.py --api-only
quarto preview docs
Preview is not a substitute for the final executable build. All lightweight examples use explicit seeds and the CPU. The optional LLM guide is labeled non-executed and does not download model weights. Figures and printed tables on the other worked pages are produced by their code, not copied manually. CI additionally checks every page in Chromium at desktop and mobile widths, including equation rendering, search, theme switching and sidebar navigation.

title: Development and documentation
text:
How publication works
Source lives on main; generated HTML and assets live on gh-pages. The docs GitHub Actions workflow builds and checks pull requests without publishing. A successful build on main (or a manual workflow run on main) commits the rendered site to gh-pages and deploys the same files through GitHub Pages. This explicit deploy step avoids relying on a second workflow being triggered by an Actions-authored branch push.
Do not hand-edit gh-pages: edit .qmd files or Python docstrings on a source branch. Once merged to main, the site is rebuilt automatically. The published build record identifies its source commit, build time and key dependency versions. The gh-pages commit message also records the source revision, so rendered changes remain inspectable and recoverable.

title: Development and documentation
text:
Adding or changing an estimator

Document its input shapes, objective, normalization, fitted attributes and failure conditions in source docstrings. Make supported inference explicit.
Add its public entry point to the Quartodoc inventory in _quarto.yml. The build rejects omissions from the package’s declared public exports.
Add a mathematical guide or extend an existing one. Include a small reproducible example, a relevant diagnostic and an explanation of the assumptions needed to interpret the estimate.
Add numerical tests that address the estimator, preferably with independent reference calculations, and run the affected tests. For broader changes run the repository suite with the test extra installed.
Run the documentation build. Inspect plots and formulas as well as exit status; a successful optimizer call need not be an informative example.

title: Development and documentation
text:
Documentation design
The site uses local/shared Quarto assets and KaTeX for mathematics. It is a multipage website, so shared assets avoid duplicating large scripts in every API page. No external font service is required. The sidebar, search and method-selection page provide complementary ways to find material.
The API reference is generated from the installed checkout, including inherited public methods. A displayed inherited method can still be unimplemented for a particular estimator: consult the method body/docstring and the guide’s inference notes. Research interfaces and numerical behavior can evolve; pin a commit and environment for a reproducible study.
